candidate.answerReason: Both assertions in B express that membership in the proposed locus implies satisfaction of the conditions. Neither establishes that every satisfying point belongs to the locus.

methods.label: Check that both directions are proved
methods.explanation:
A locus must contain all the points satisfying the conditions and no other points. Let \(L\) mean that a point belongs to the proposed figure, and let \(S\) mean that it satisfies the conditions. We must establish both
\[
L\Rightarrow S
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
S\Rightarrow L.
\]
The assertion \(L\Rightarrow S\) rules out a point that is on the figure but fails the conditions. Saying that every point failing the conditions is off the figure rules out exactly the same possibility. These are equivalent statements, called contrapositives.

In B, the first assertion is \(\neg S\Rightarrow\neg L\), and the second is \(L\Rightarrow S\). They therefore prove the same direction twice. They do not show that every satisfying point has been included.

For example, suppose the condition is being one unit from a fixed point. Taking only the upper semicircle satisfies both assertions in B, but it omits the lower semicircle, whose points also satisfy the condition.

C states both required directions directly. A and E each replace one direction by its contrapositive, while D uses the contrapositives of both directions. Thus B is the incorrect proof method, choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
methods.levelReason: Elementary implications, contrapositives, and a geometric counterexample explain the logical distinction.
